summary: Benioff argues the SaaS sector re-rating is cyclical, not structural — Salesforce's strong fundamentals ($46B+ revenue, $16B+ cash flow, massive buyback) plus new AI-driven efficiencies via coding agents and AgentForce position the company to thrive through the downturn.
quote: we'll do over $46 billion this year, more than $16 billion in cash flow. We have more than 83,000 employees. These are the things that I'm focused on.

summary: Chamath argues that large, entrenched enterprise software companies like Salesforce are safe from AI disruption at the high end of the market, and that as AI hype deflates, buyers will need trusted incumbents to monetize AI tokens — setting up a re-rating reversal.
quote: The high end of the market where Marc operates, where the large monoliths operate is quite safe. And the tell was this week, the deployment company deal basically shows you what OpenAI is running into.

summary: Benioff argues Anthropic's bet on coding agents proved correct, making it a rocket ship that won't stop — and he is spending ~$300M on Anthropic tokens at Salesforce this year, treating it as the clear leader in enterprise AI coding.
quote: Have you seen Anthropic? I mean, it is a rocket ship. That will not stop because you can use this product to do these incredible, amazing things.

summary: Chamath views Anthropic's pivot to coding agents as the winning strategy among AI labs, citing that its deployment deal with a Big 4 firm reveals the high end of the enterprise market is harder to crack than expected — validating Anthropic's entrenched position with real workloads.
quote: The deployment company deal basically shows you what OpenAI is running into... at the high end of the market where all the action is, what people are finding is, hey, hold on a second, this is a lot harder than we thought.

summary: Friedberg is skeptical of OpenAI's ability to sustain long-term partnerships, noting the strained Apple relationship as one in a pattern of partnership failures.
quote: I don't know what to tell you. This— there doesn't seem to be a lot of long-term partnerships with OpenAI.

scoreNote: Named as explicit pick ('my choice for the next year') in context of AI positioning discussion.
summary: Jason argues Apple has the clearest path to becoming a top AI player via local models on its extraordinary hardware, and names it as his pick for the next year.
quote: Apple has the clearest path to becoming, you know, a top 2 or 3 player in AI simply by buying something like Perplexity or Mistral... I think Apple's my choice for the next year.

summary: Friedberg argues Apple's massive install base in personal data (mail, calendar, photos) gives it a strong foundation to build a killer personal AI assistant, though it will face formidable competition from Google.
quote: Apple obviously has an embedded install piece. How many people are using Apple services for doing all of their mail, for calendaring, for storing their information?... billions. Yeah. So that may end up becoming kind of the way that the

summary: Friedberg argues Google has a real opportunity to dominate the AI assistant interface by integrating Gemini deeply with its personal and enterprise data ecosystem (Gmail, Drive, Photos, G Suite), becoming a formidable competitor.
quote: Google has a real opportunity to integrate a Gemini assistant into all of your personal information in Gemini and Calendar, your Google Drive, your Google Photos, where all of your personal information sits.

summary: Chamath argues the US should sell advanced chips to China specifically to ensure Nvidia wins the AI chip race rather than ceding ground to Huawei.

summary: Chamath argues the low end and vertical SaaS market is essentially finished due to AI disruption, with no safe space remaining for small or mid-market software companies.
quote: I think the low end of the market is basically finished. I think there is no safe space. I think the high end of the market where Marc operates, where the large monoliths operate is quite safe.
